Hydrophobia is a noun that means an extreme, abnormal fear of water. It refers to a condition where a person (or animal) has a powerful, overwhelming dread of water — not just a mild dislike, but a deep, uncontrollable terror that goes far beyond what is reasonable or rational.
The Two Ways This Word Is Used

This word carries two distinct but closely connected meanings, and understanding both is essential.

Meaning 1: A Phobia (a Psychological Fear of Water)

In general use, hydrophobia refers to an irrational phobia — a specific type of anxiety disorder — where someone has an intense, persistent fear of water. This goes well beyond simply being nervous around deep water or not knowing how to swim.

A person with hydrophobia might be terrified of:

  • Drinking water or any liquid
  • Touching water
  • Seeing a large body of water like a lake or river
  • Even hearing the sound of running water

The fear is disproportionate — meaning the level of panic the person feels is wildly out of proportion to any actual danger the water poses. The person usually knows the fear is unreasonable, but they simply cannot control it. This causes serious distress and disrupts daily life — something as ordinary as taking a shower or drinking a glass of water can feel impossible.

This use of hydrophobia is essentially a synonym for aquaphobia (another word for the fear of water), though hydrophobia tends to carry a slightly more clinical, serious tone.

Meaning 2: A Symptom of Rabies (and Sometimes, Rabies Itself)

This is the older, medical meaning of the word, and historically it is the primary reason the word became so well-known.

Rabies is a deadly viral disease that attacks the brain and nervous system. It is transmitted through the bite of an infected animal (most famously, dogs). One of the most terrifying and distinctive symptoms of rabies — especially in its advanced stages — is a violent, painful aversion to water. Here is exactly what happens and why:

  • Rabies severely damages the parts of the brain and nervous system that control swallowing.
  • When a rabies patient tries to drink water, the muscles in their throat go into agonizing, uncontrollable spasms. Swallowing becomes not just difficult but excruciatingly painful.
  • Because of this, the patient's brain begins to associate water with unbearable pain, creating what looks and functions exactly like an extreme phobia.
  • Eventually, even the sight, sound, or mention of water — or even a breeze of air on the skin — is enough to trigger these violent spasms and fits of panic.

Because this fear-of-water symptom was so striking and so consistent in rabies patients, doctors throughout history used hydrophobia as a medical synonym for rabies itself. If someone was said to have hydrophobia in older medical texts or literature, it almost always meant they had rabies.

So in this second meaning:

  • Hydrophobia = rabies (the disease)
  • Or more precisely: hydrophobia = the water-terror symptom caused by rabies
How the Two Meanings Are Related

The connection is not a coincidence. Both meanings describe the same observable experience — an overwhelming, pathological terror of water — just with different causes:

CauseCondition called
Psychological / anxiety disorderHydrophobia (a phobia)
Rabies virus attacking the brainHydrophobia (rabies symptom / rabies itself)

In both cases, the person is not choosing to fear water. The fear is real, physical, and completely beyond their voluntary control.

• In everyday language and psychology, hydrophobia refers to the phobia — an irrational fear of water.
  • In medical and historical contexts, especially older texts, hydrophobia refers to rabies or its water-aversion symptom.
  • In modern medicine, doctors now almost always use the word rabies directly, and hydrophobia is used mainly to describe that specific symptom of it.

So context is everything. If you see this word in a psychology book, it means a fear-based disorder. If you see it in a historical novel or old medical record, it almost certainly means rabies.

• "The doctor noted that the patient's hydrophobia — his violent reaction to the sight of a glass of water — confirmed the rabies diagnosis."
  • "She had suffered from hydrophobia since childhood and could not even approach a swimming pool without experiencing a panic attack."
  • "In the 19th century, a person bitten by a rabid dog and later showing signs of hydrophobia was considered beyond saving."
The Single Most Important Thing to Remember

If you remember nothing else: hydrophobia = an extreme, uncontrollable fear of water. Whether that fear comes from a psychological disorder or from the brain being ravaged by rabies, the word captures the same terrifying reality — that something as simple and life-giving as water has become a source of absolute dread.
